The 30 g/day reading is confirmed correct: Methods defines the subgroup as "≥ 30 g/d," Table 1 headers it the same way, and Table 2's per-study doses are all gram-scale (30 g/day, 24 g/day, 20 g/day, 30.5 g/day, etc.) -- nowhere near milligram range. The source paper's Discussion and Conclusion nonetheless repeat "30 mg/day," a real uncorrected error, not an abstract-only artifact. UNRESOLVED: the subgroup statistic is printed as WMD -0.01 with 95% CI -0.10 to -0.08 (n=5 studies), an interval that excludes its own point estimate; full text gives no way to determine the correct figures. SEPARATE INCONSISTENCY: Table 1 defines duration subgroups as ≥4 weeks / <4 weeks, but the Discussion/Conclusion instead describe the significant effect as occurring in interventions "less than 2 weeks" -- a cutoff absent from the paper's own methodology. Flag this if this row is ever used for a duration-based judgment, not just dose.

outcome_measured: antibiotic-associated diarrhoea prevention in children
notes: VERIFIED against PubMed 2026-09-27, replacing the unverified 2026-09-07 row that set no range. Range set by Vanderhoof 1999 (PMID 10547243), a double-blind randomised trial of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea prevention in children aged 6 months to 10 years, n=202 enrolled and 188 completing, dosing 1x10^10 to 2x10^10 CFU/day. 25 placebo-treated versus 7 LGG-treated children had diarrhoea, and LGG significantly reduced stool frequency and increased consistency by day 10. Author affiliations are University of Nebraska paediatrics only; the funding statement was not verifiable from the abstract and is recorded as unverified rather than asserted independent. CONTESTED: the Cochrane review of probiotics for acute infectious diarrhoea (Collinson 2020, PMID 33295643, 82 studies and 12,127 participants, 11,526 of them children) found probiotics probably make little or no difference to the number of people with diarrhoea lasting 48 hours or longer, with LGG examined in a pre-specified subgroup. Recorded under the contested-literature rule; it does not set the range, since ranges come from positive-outcome trials, but a reader should weigh it against this row

IBS symptom relief: abdominal pain, bloating, gas
notes: range set by the two positive-outcome trials of this strain, both manufacturer-linked. Whorwell 2006 (PMID 16863564, n=362 women with IBS) is the pivotal encapsulated dose-ranging trial: 1x10^8 CFU/day significantly superior to placebo for abdominal pain, composite score, bloating, bowel dysfunction, incomplete evacuation, straining and passage of gas, while 1x10^6 and 1x10^10 were NOT different from placebo. Dose response is therefore non-monotonic and 1x10^8 is the only capsule dose shown to work. O'Mahony 2005 (PMID 15765388, n=77) found 1x10^10 CFU/day effective but delivered in a malted milk drink, not a capsule, so it does not establish 1x10^10 for an encapsulated product. INDEPENDENCE: both trials carry authors affiliated with the manufacturer (Charbonneau, Procter & Gamble, on Whorwell 2006; Kiely, Alimentary Health, on both). They set the range only because no independent positive trial was identified, and are flagged here as the weaker basis. CONTESTED: an independent meta-analysis (Yuan 2017, PMID 28166427) found single-strain B. infantis 35624 did not significantly affect abdominal pain, bloating/distention or bowel habit satisfaction; recorded per the contested-literature rule but does not set the range. PubMed searched 2026-10-26; these are the only human trials of the cocktail indexed.
